rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Damagha can mean overcoming or vanquishing, but evokes skull-crushing to the brain and can also mean stamping a form into soft material.
rows.anchor: Crushes renders the verb damagha, a word that can have the general sense of overcoming or vanquishing

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Ṭ understands vanishing as meaning that falsehood is destroyed.
rows.anchor: Vanishes is understood by some to mean “is destroyed” (Ṭ).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran discusses the relationship between truth and falsehood elsewhere, including truth's triumph and God's verification of truth.
rows.anchor: The relationship between falsehood and truth in the Quran is discussed at greater length in the commentary on 17:81

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: That which the wrongdoers describe may refer to the lies they tell.
rows.anchor: That which you describe can either refer to the lies the wrongdoers told

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the phrase may refer to idolatry and the partners attributed to God.
rows.anchor: or signify their idolatry, recalling phrases such as Exalted is God above the partners they ascribe

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The indictment also recalls the closing appeal to God for help against what people ascribe to Him.

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some understand the descriptions as the accusations against the Prophet in verses 3–5.
rows.anchor: Some understand these descriptions to refer to the accusations made against the Prophet in vv. 3–5.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Commentators usually understand these verses as referring to idols and false gods, often described as neither harming nor benefiting their worshippers.
rows.anchor: These verses are usually thought to refer to idols and false gods, which are often described as something that neither harms nor benefits

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some read verse 13 as referring to help sought from worldly powers.
rows.anchor: Some say v. 13 refers to the help one seeks from worldly powers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage could still refer to idols, since idolatry itself harms by diverting worship from the One God.
rows.anchor: but this could also refer to idols, because the worship of idols, far from being innocuous, is considered, from a religious perspective, to be harmful in itself

rows.speaker: most commentators
rows.claim: Most commentators classify al-Shuʿarāʾ as a Makkan sūrah.
rows.anchor: commentators al-Shuʿarāʾ is a Makkan

rows.speaker: Āl, Q, Ṭs
rows.claim: Āl, Q, and Ṭs consider verses 224–227 Madinan.
rows.anchor: some think a small number of verses (vv. 224–27) are Madinan (Āl, Q, Ṭs)

rows.speaker: Āl
rows.claim: Āl also includes verse 197 among the Madinan verses.
rows.anchor: others include v. 197 among the Madinan verses (Āl).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah takes its name from shuʿarāʾ, the poets, whose role endured from pre-Islamic Arab culture into the Islamic era in altered form.
rows.anchor: role in pre-Islamic Arab culture, a role that endured during the Islamic era, but in a different form

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first narrative recounts Moses' confrontation with Pharaoh, the sorcerers, and the Israelites' flight from Egypt.
rows.anchor: partial telling of the account of Moses’ confrontation with Pharaoh, his duel with the sorcerers, and the flight from Egypt

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The next account concerns Abraham, his idolatrous people, and his prayer that God forgive his father.
rows.anchor: This section is followed by an account of Abraham (vv. 69–89) and his idolatrous people, and Abraham’s prayer of forgiveness for his father.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Noah's story stresses his people's aversion to followers of low social status.
rows.anchor: Next told is Noah’s story (vv. 105–21), with emphasis on his people’s aversion to the individuals of low social status who followed him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hūd's people pursue domination and worldly glory, while Ṣāliḥ's people are marked by material attachments.
rows.anchor: stories of Hūd (vv. 123–39), whose people are condemned for their pursuit of domination and worldly glory, and Ṣāliḥ (vv. 141–58), whose people are characterized by their material attachments

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah gives brief accounts of Lot and Shuʿayb.
rows.anchor: and brief accounts of Lot (vv. 160–73) and Shuʿayb (vv. 176–89).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The final section affirms that the Quran is revealed from a spiritual source.
rows.anchor: affirmation that the Quran is indeed revealed from a spiritual source (v. 193)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran is revealed in Arabic to a people meant to understand and comprehend it.
rows.anchor: it was revealed in Arabic to a people who are meant to understand and comprehend it (vv. 197–200)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah denies that satans or jinn brought the Quran and says they are barred from hearing it.
rows.anchor: no satan or jinn could have brought the Quran (vv. 210–212)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Poets' words were often attributed to a supernatural source in satans or jinn.
rows.anchor: whose words were often considered to have a magical or supernatural origin in satans or jinn

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Unlike poetry's alleged supernatural source, the Quran originates with God and was revealed through Gabriel.
rows.anchor: unlike the Quran, whose origin is God and which was revealed through the Archangel Gabriel.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah uses rhythmic, poetic form and repeated refrains around prophetic stories to show their shared teachings and challenges.
rows.anchor: linking them together by showing that the fundamental teachings (and challenges) of the prophets were the same.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The story's opening parallels the formula used for other prophets' stories.
rows.anchor: For a similar opening to other prophets’ stories, cf. vv. 105–9, 123–27, 141–45, 160–64.

rows.claim: For further discussion of Shuʿayb, the commentary points to 7:85.

rows.anchor: or a group of trees (Ṭ).

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: The thicket's inhabitants may have been part of Midian or a separate people to whom Shuʿayb was sent.
rows.anchor: either part of the people of Midian or a separate people to whom Shuʿayb was sent as a prophet (Q)

rows.speaker: Al-Thaʿlabī
rows.claim: Al-Thaʿlabī argues that the thicket's people were separate because Shuʿayb is called Midian's brother in 29:36 but not here; he was from Midian.
rows.anchor: Al-Thaʿlabī argues that since Shuʿayb is described as being sent to the people of Midian as their brother (29:36)

rows.speaker: Ṭ, Th
rows.claim: These verses prohibit cheating in buying and selling.
rows.anchor: These verses instruct people not to cheat in matters of buying and selling (Ṭ, Th)

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: The corrupt conduct also includes highway robbery, piracy, raiding, and destroying crops.
rows.anchor: usually understood to include highway robbery and piracy, raiding, and the destruction of crops (R)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Midianites were guilty of corrupt, predatory commercial practices, discussed at 7:85 and 11:84–86.
rows.anchor: On the corrupt and predatory mercantile practices of which the Midianites were guilty, see 7:85c; 11:84–86c.

rows.anchor: commentators consider al-Qaṣaṣ to be an entirely

rows.anchor: some consider vv. 52–55 to be Madinan (JJ, Q)

rows.claim: Āl, IJ, and JJ place verse 85 during Muhammad's migration from Makkah to Madinah.
rows.anchor: others maintain that v. 85 was revealed during Muhammad’s migration from Makkah to Madinah (Āl, IJ, JJ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah takes its name from the story Moses tells his future father-in-law about fleeing Egypt.
rows.anchor: It takes its name from the story (qaṣaṣ) Moses tells his future father-in-law in v. 25 regarding his flight from Egypt.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening account covers Israelite oppression, Moses' mother placing him in the river, his rescue and care by Pharaoh's family, and reunion with his mother.
rows.anchor: the story of Moses and Pharaoh and describes the oppression suffered by the Children of Israel, leading Moses’ mother to cast him into the river

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses kills an Egyptian quarreling with an Israelite, then flees Egypt for Midian.
rows.anchor: striking and killing an Egyptian who was quarreling with an Israelite and the subsequent flight of Moses from Egypt to Midian (vv. 14–22)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In Midian, Moses meets two sisters, marries one, and spends years working for his father-in-law.
rows.anchor: There Moses meets two sisters, one of whom he will come to marry, and finds refuge for many years in the employ of his father-in-law

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses encounters the fire, hears God, witnesses his first miracles, and asks that Aaron join him against Pharaoh.
rows.anchor: Then Moses encounters the fire from which he hears God speak to him; he has his first experience of the miracles

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The confrontation includes Pharaoh's claim to divinity and his boast of building a structure to climb toward Heaven.
rows.anchor: issue of the latter’s claim to divinity and his boast about building a structure

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muhammad is reminded he did not witness Moses' revelations; prophets sent meanwhile expose contemporaries' pride as they sought guidance but rejected the messenger.
rows.anchor: The Prophet Muhammad is told that he was not present when Moses received his revelations

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who hear the truth and believe contrast with the rejecting contemporaries.
rows.anchor: They are contrasted with those who, when they hear the truth, believe in it (vv. 51–55).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The final section emphasizes the world's ephemerality in relation to the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: The last part of the sūrah emphasizes the ephemerality of the world in relation to the Hereafter

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses' contemporary Korah exemplifies wickedness, worldly extravagance, and pride.
rows.anchor: Moses’ contemporary Korah is presented as the epitome of wickedness and worldly extravagance and pride.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The conclusion says this world will end and all things return to God.
rows.anchor: reminder that this world is coming to an end and that all things will return to God (vv. 56–88).
